bls-atus.name: American Time Use Survey, household activities
bls-atus.outcome: Women averaged 2.38 hours a day on household activities and men 1.58 (1.99 overall); food preparation and cleanup took women 0.91 hours a day and men 0.51
bls-atus.limits: National averages across everyone, including people who did none that day; says nothing about any one household.
bls-atus.locator: Chart: Average hours per day spent in selected household activities, 2025 annual averages

energystar-dishwasher.name: ENERGY STAR dishwasher guidance
energystar-dishwasher.outcome: A new certified dishwasher uses less than half the energy of washing by hand, saves 8,400 gallons of water and over 230 hours of personal time a year; scrape plates instead of pre-rinsing
energystar-dishwasher.limits: Federal program estimate comparing a new certified model with hand washing every day; older machines and smaller households save less.
energystar-dishwasher.locator: "save you over 230 hours of personal time over the course of a year"

cr-robovac.name: Consumer Reports robot vacuum tests
cr-robovac.outcome: Three robot vacuums under $300 rated near the top; best for daily pickups in uncluttered rooms with bare floors or low-pile carpet
cr-robovac.limits: 2018 tests; models and prices have changed. Clutter, cords and thick rugs get in the way, and a robot is not a deep clean.
cr-robovac.locator: "daily pickups" in uncluttered rooms; full-size vacuum for deep cleaning

nutrinet-planning.name: NutriNet-Santé meal planning study
nutrinet-planning.outcome: Among 40,554 French adults, people who planned meals ahead had more varied diets, and women who planned had lower odds of obesity
nutrinet-planning.limits: Cross-sectional: shows an association, not cause, and does not measure time saved.
nutrinet-planning.locator: "Meal planning could be a potential tool to offset time scarcity"

aap-chores.name: American Academy of Pediatrics, chores and responsibility
aap-chores.outcome: Children 5 to 7 can make and pack school lunches; 8 to 10 can help make dinner and put away their own laundry; 11 to 12 can cook a simple meal with supervision and do and fold laundry
aap-chores.limits: General guidance adapted from a pediatrics book; children vary.

pew-housework.name: Pew Research Center study of marriages where spouses earn about the same
pew-housework.outcome: In marriages where both spouses earn about the same, wives spend 4.6 hours a week on housework and husbands about two
pew-housework.limits: Opposite-sex marriages only; averages from national time-use data.

fair-play.name: Fair Play by Eve Rodsky
fair-play.outcome: A method that lists 100 household tasks as cards, so each partner owns whole tasks, divided fairly rather than equally
fair-play.limits: A self-help book method (2021 is the paperback date); no trial results.

daminger.name: Allison Daminger, The Cognitive Dimension of Household Labor
daminger.outcome: In 26 of 32 couples, women did more of the thinking work of a home: anticipating needs, identifying options, deciding and monitoring; men joined mostly at the deciding step
daminger.limits: Interviews with 70 middle- and upper-middle-class people in 35 couples; not a representative sample.

birmingham-coop.name: Birmingham dinner co-op
birmingham-coop.outcome: Three families each cook one large meal that feeds all three, and swap the shares on Sundays; they have done this for more than a decade
birmingham-coop.limits: One group of friends; the article gives no year and no measured time saved.

nstreet-cohousing.name: N Street Cohousing
nstreet-cohousing.outcome: Neighbors took down backyard fences one house at a time from 1986; now 19 houses, about 50 residents; shared dinners one or more times a week; regulars cook with a partner about once a month; around $3 a plate
nstreet-cohousing.limits: One community of owners who chose this; house counts differ slightly between the group's own pages (history page: https://nstreetcohousing.org/our-history/).
nstreet-cohousing.locator: "one with a partner once a month or every ten meals eaten"

meal-train.name: Meal Train
meal-train.outcome: A free page where friends pick dates to bring meals after a birth, surgery, loss, illness or job loss, with an optional fund for groceries
meal-train.limits: Works only if enough people sign up; meant for a hard stretch, not forever.

meals-on-wheels.name: Meals on Wheels America
meals-on-wheels.outcome: 244 million meals a year to 2.6 million older adults; one in three local providers has a waitlist, averaging four months
meals-on-wheels.limits: Local programs set eligibility, usually 60 or older and homebound; waitlists are common.

si-se-puede.name: Sí Se Puede Women's Cooperative
si-se-puede.outcome: A worker-owned house-cleaning co-op that grew from 15 to 67 members; one member who earned $8 an hour cleaning alone now averages about $20
si-se-puede.limits: One co-op in New York City; membership numbers vary by date.

alia.name: Alia, from the National Domestic Workers Alliance
alia.outcome: An online tool where house-cleaning clients add a suggested $5 per cleaning toward the cleaner's paid time off and insurance
alia.limits: Described in a 2019 article; current terms and states covered were not checked.

sweden-rut.name: Sweden's RUT deduction for household services
sweden-rut.outcome: Households, including renters, deduct 50 percent of the labor cost of cleaning, laundry and similar work, up to 75,000 kronor a year combined with home repairs; the company files the claim
sweden-rut.limits: 2021 article; caps change. Contested: public money goes to households that buy help; who benefits most was not checked in this run.
sweden-rut.locator: "you can claim 50 percent of the cost of labour"

belgium-vouchers.name: Belgium's service vouchers (titres-services)
belgium-vouchers.outcome: Publicly subsidized vouchers, one per hour of household help such as cleaning, ironing and cooking; in 2023 about €9 an hour in Flanders and Wallonia and €10 in Brussels; Brussels workers earn at least €13.10 an hour
belgium-vouchers.limits: Prices rise over time and differ by region; public cost not given in the article.
belgium-vouchers.locator: "Service vouchers were launched as a solution in 2004"

us-school-meals.name: States with free school lunch for all students
us-school-meals.outcome: As of 2025 to 2026, California, Colorado, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Mexico, New York and Vermont give free lunch to all public school students with no application
us-school-meals.limits: A consumer guide updated August 2025; other schools may still be free through the federal Community Eligibility Provision.
us-school-meals.locator: "There’s no need to apply or provide income information."

finland-meals.name: Finland's free school meals
finland-meals.outcome: A law on free school meals took effect in 1943 and the rest of Finland followed by 1948; Helsinki now cooks lunch every weekday for about 44,000 students in 140 schools at roughly €2.50 a meal
finland-meals.limits: City of Helsinki's own page; costs differ across Finnish towns.
finland-meals.locator: "The act on free meals for schoolchildren entered into force in 1943"

iceland-1975.name: Iceland Women's Day Off
iceland-1975.outcome: On October 24, 1975, about 90 percent of women stopped paid work, housework and child care for the day; about 25,000 gathered in Reykjavik out of a population of roughly 220,000; Vigdís Finnbogadóttir was elected president in 1980
iceland-1975.limits: The 90 percent figure is the organizers' estimate.
iceland-1975.locator: "no housework or child-rearing" for the whole day

wages-housework.name: Wages for Housework campaign
wages-housework.outcome: Started in 1972 by Mariarosa Dalla Costa, Silvia Federici, Brigitte Galtier and Selma James; by 2025 about 118 million women in twelve Indian states received cash transfers, some justified as pay for housework
wages-housework.limits: A contested demand; many people oppose paying for housework from public money.
wages-housework.locator: History section; India cash transfers estimate attributed to the BBC

japan-soji.name: Student cleaning time in Japanese schools
japan-soji.outcome: Students in small groups take turns cleaning classrooms, corridors, the gym and the entrance hall, usually at lunch break or after school, with a deeper o-soji at the end of each term
japan-soji.limits: A teaching resource describing a general custom; practice varies by school, and schools still have custodial staff.
japan-soji.locator: each han "takes turns cleaning a designated area every week"
